newsitem.title: MEXICO: INTERVIEW - Avantel sees net profits by 1998.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Avantel sees net profits by 1998.

text.p: Telephone company Avantel could see net profits from its operations in Mexico's recently opened long distance market by 1998, the company's chief financial officer said in an interview.
"This will probably come about in the second half of 1998, by the final quarter of 1998 we think there will then be earnings," said Avantel CFO Jose Maria Zubiria.
Zubiria said the company had originally expected to see net figures in the black within three to five years following their entry into the long-distance market on Jan. 1, 1997.
Avantel is a joint venture between Mexican financial group Banamex-Accival and U.S.-based MCI Communications Corp.
Avantel is currently transmitting two million minutes of long-distance traffic per day along a 5,400-kilometre (3,350 miles) optic fibre network, Zubiria said.
The company aimed to generate net earnings through growth in traffic and a financial strategy aimed at reducing the burden of past and future investment, he added.

Avantel has already covered the cost of its initial $1 billion in investments, Zubiria said, using a $481 million loan granted by the Canadian Eximbank and Export Development Corp. Payment on the loan will begin in 1999, by which time Avantel expects to have free cash flow, he said.
The loan was granted in February 1997, and Avantel has received $218 million to cover $150 million in bridge loans. The average interest payable on the 13-year loan will be less than nine percent.

"Network growth will require further investment which may take place in 1998 or 1999, by which time we we will have cash flow to back up our investment, and then our financing plans will certainly continue," Zubiria said.
Zubiria thought Avantel's most formidable stumbling block could be interconnection charges levied by former monopoly Telmex.
"For each peso we take in, more than 50 centavos are used to pay interconnection charges... This is much greater than international standards," he said.
"If they were at international levels, we could pass some reduction in costs on to clients, or even a larger investment for Avantel," he added.

Nonetheless, new entrants to the long-distance market have no choice other than to interconnect with Telmex, so Zubiria said the only alternative for Avantel was to promote competition in the local market.
For this reason the company was holding talks with Spanish telecomms firm Telefonica de Espana, he said.
